tested_scope: Bounded documentation-level test of whether a content-addressed Git commit/tree/blob inside a GitHub public fork network can serve as a provider-retained minimum-generation/incarnation witness after branch rewind or one repository/fork deletion, without an independently administered repository or richer-mode/protected/manual execution.

public_sources.title: GitHub Docs — Deleting a repository
public_sources.observation: GitHub documents that deleting a public repository does not delete its public forks; deleted repositories may be restorable only within a bounded window, and some fork-network restoration can require GitHub Support on a paid plan.

public_sources.title: GitHub Docs — Forks
public_sources.observation: GitHub documents that when a public upstream is deleted an active public fork can become the new upstream, and that commits from a deleted fork can remain accessible in the repository network. This is network-survival behavior, not an indefinite retention guarantee for every unreachable object after the network becomes empty.

public_sources.title: GitHub Docs — Troubleshooting commits
public_sources.observation: GitHub documents that a commit may still be visible on GitHub after its branch was deleted or force-pushed, but recovery guidance relies on a collaborator who still has the commit locally pushing a new branch. The documentation does not promise indefinite provider retention or discoverability of an unreachable commit solely from its SHA.

public_sources.title: GitHub Docs — Git database REST API
public_sources.observation: The API exposes get-by-SHA operations for Git objects that exist in a repository Git database, but the endpoint documentation does not establish an anti-garbage-collection or permanent-retention contract for objects that become unreachable from all repository refs/networks.

public_sources.title: GitHub Docs — About protected branches
public_sources.observation: GitHub documents that force pushes can remove commits from branch history and can delete or repoint branches when allowed; a known commit SHA therefore is not itself a monotonic branch-authority witness.

bounded_case_matrix.authority_effect: A network copy can survive one repository deletion, but this only moves the live upstream inside the same fork network.
The SHA can identify an old object if GitHub still retains/exposes it, but current official documentation does not make that continued availability a durable monotonicity contract.

No official guarantee found that an unreachable commit/tree/blob remains indefinitely addressable after the entire live network is gone; deleted-repository restoration is bounded and can involve a paid-support path.

Content addressing proves identity only after the SHA is known; the tested provider documentation does not supply a zero-dependency monotonic index that reconstructs the newest witness SHA after both repository refs and role-local state roll back.

A repository name is reusable while a Git object SHA names content, not the new repository incarnation; no tested provider primitive automatically rejects a newly created same-name repository as an older authority generation.
Lightweight repository API access can transport evidence, but temporary unavailability cannot be treated as proof that the witness is absent or current.

observed_from_official_docs: A public repository deletion does not delete public forks.
An active public fork can become the new upstream after public-upstream deletion.
Commits can remain accessible in a repository network after a fork is deleted.
Force-push or branch deletion can remove a commit from branch history while the commit may still be visible on GitHub.
Deleted-repository restoration is bounded rather than a stated permanent object-retention service.
observation_vs_inference.inference_limited_to_tested_scope: Because no official source in this bounded probe guarantees indefinite retention plus deterministic discoverability of an unreachable Git object after the entire fork network disappears, a bare content-addressed commit/tree/blob cannot be accepted as a provider-enforced minimum-generation/incarnation witness for rollback safety. This is a documentation-scope falsification, not a claim that GitHub immediately garbage-collects such objects or that no undocumented retention exists.

phase1_result.new_falsification: Content addressing supplies immutable identity but not a documented provider-level liveness/discoverability guarantee. Fork-network survival covers one-repository deletion only while another live network member remains; it does not establish the required witness after network-empty deletion, own-state rollback that loses the SHA, or delete/recreate incarnation change.
phase1_result.minimal_unresolved_child: A provider-enforced repository-local monotonic witness whose newest version is reconstructible after refs plus role-local state roll back, survives same-principal repository deletion/recreation or otherwise rejects the new incarnation, and requires no second administrator/principal, protected/manual setup, finite paid quota, or incremental cost.

zero_dependency_zero_quota_assessment.candidate_acceptance_blocker: documented provider retention/discoverability and incarnation-binding guarantees are insufficient

conflict_check: Role-local Part88 only; no other worker state, downstream state, O state, shared execution ledger, other-role receipt/config, or protected authority read or modified.
frontier: Provider-enforced immutable release/tag policy as a possible repository-local monotonic witness.
Provider event/audit surfaces are only relevant if retention, zero-quota availability and same-principal anti-rollback are sufficient; otherwise remain unresolved.
Any candidate must reconstruct the newest witness after local-state rollback rather than merely authenticate a caller-supplied old SHA.
exact_continuation: Part89: execute exactly one bounded GitHub immutable-release/tag witness leaf using official GitHub documentation plus own clean state only. Test whether immutable releases or provider-enforced tag immutability can supply a repository-local monotonic minimum-generation/incarnation witness without an independent administrator. Required negatives: repository admin disabling the rule, release/tag deletion, repository delete/recreate, same-name incarnation reuse, force-push/reference mutation outside the release path, loss of local newest-version pointer, API/rate-limit interruption, any plan/feature quota or paid-support dependency. Accept only if the newest witness remains provider-enforced, reconstructible and rollback-resistant under the same principal with zero optional monthly/trial/paid quota and zero incremental cost; otherwise persist the exact authority or discoverability gap.
